old:
unrelenting
the fear comes back
new:
unrelenting
that the fear comes back
why: Inf. I 5-6 'esta selva selvaggia e aspra e forte / che nel pensier rinova la paura'; without the connective the two lines run on (Longfellow: 'Which in the very thought renews the fear').

old: faint, hoarse from long silence
new: faint from long silence
why: Inf. I 63 'chi per lungo silenzio parea fioco': one word; giving both readings is a doubled gloss.

old: that low Italy
new: that humble Italy
why: Inf. I 106 'umile Italia', after Aeneid III 522 humilem Italiam: humble, low-lying; in current English 'low' alone reads as a value judgment.

old: you ruined souls!
new: you wicked souls!
why: Inf. III 84 'Guai a voi, anime prave!' (Longfellow: 'ye souls depraved'); 'ruined' makes them victims.

old: throw themselves down from that bank
new: casts itself down from that bank
why: Collective 'seed' with plural verb trips aloud; Dante 'gittansi' (III 116) is plural by sense, English wants agreement.

old:
The honored name of them
that still rings of them up in your life
wins grace in Heaven,
new:
The honor of their name,
which still resounds up there in your life,
wins grace in Heaven,
why: Inf. IV 76-78 'L'onrata nominanza / che di lor suona sù ne la tua vita, / grazia acquista nel ciel che sì li avanza'; 'of them … of them' tangles the line.

old:
because they were not baptized,
the gateway into the faith you hold.
new:
because they had no baptism,
which is the gateway to the faith you hold.
why: Inf. IV 35-36 'ch'ei non ebber battesmo, / ch'è porta de la fede che tu credi': baptism is the gate; the appositive dangled off a verb.

old: that she followed Ninus
new: that she succeeded Ninus
why: Inf. V 59 'che succedette a Nino' (Longfellow: 'succeeded Ninus'); 'followed' reads as trailing after him.

old: wheeling and battering, it gives them no peace.
new: and wheeling and battering them, gives them no peace.
why: Comma splice; Dante V 33 'voltando e percotendo li molesta' is one clause.

old: it had shut down before the pity
new: it had closed before the pity
why: Inf. VI 2 'che si chiuse dinanzi a la pietà'; 'shut down' now reads as machinery or therapy-speak.

old: the party from the woods
new: the rustic party
why: Inf. VI 65 'la parte selvaggia', the country-bred Whites (Longfellow: 'the rustic party'); 'from the woods' literalizes a political label into a place.

old: "You come alone. Let him go —
new: "You come alone, and let him go away —
why: Inf. VIII 89 'Vien tu solo, e quei sen vada'; 'Let him go' now reads as 'release him'.

old: "Down into this sad pit of a shell,
new: "Down into the bottom of this sad hollow,
why: Inf. IX 16 'In questo fondo de la trista conca' (Longfellow: 'this bottom of the dismal shell'); 'pit of a shell' stacks two images and catches aloud.

old: speaking so plainly,
new: speaking so courteously,
why: Inf. X 23 'parlando così onesto' is decorously, courteously (Longfellow: 'modestly'); Farinata praises Dante's manners, not his plainness.

old: and you yourself have inclined me to that."
new: and not only now have you inclined me to that."
why: Inf. X 21 'e tu m'hai non pur mo a ciò disposto': 'not only now' (cf. III 76-78) was dropped.

old: there is no help for it — he must repent,
new: he must repent, and all to no avail,
why: Inf. XI 42 'convien che sanza pro si penta' (Longfellow: 'Must needs without avail repent'); 'no help for it' reads as 'unavoidably' and loses the futility.

old:
"Yes, he's alive, and alive alone
it's my task
new:
"Yes, he's alive, and he is all alone;
it's my task
why: Inf. XII 85-86 'Ben è vivo, e sì soletto / mostrar li mi convien la valle buia'; 'alive alone' is garbled.

old: schooled by your sister and her thread.
new: schooled by your sister.
why: Inf. XII 20 'ammaestrato da la tua sorella': 'and her thread' is an explanatory gloss added to the line.

old: naked and clawed,
new: naked and scratched,
why: Inf. XIII 116 'nudi e graffiati' (Longfellow: 'naked and scratched'); 'clawed' reads as having claws, like the Harpies just described.

old:
When the savage soul tears itself loose
from the body it ripped itself away from,
new:
When the savage soul departs
from the body it has torn itself away from,
why: Inf. XIII 94-95 'Quando si parte l'anima feroce / dal corpo ond' ella stessa s'è disvelta': departs, then uprooted; the Lectio says the tearing twice.

old:
"Follow your star,
and you cannot fail
new:
"If you follow your star,
you cannot fail
why: Inf. XV 55 'Se tu segui tua stella' is conditional (Longfellow: 'If thou thy star do follow'); the imperative makes Brunetto preach where he predicts.

old: God, the wounds I saw
new: Ah, the wounds I saw
why: Inf. XVI 10 'Ahimè'. Policy: Dante's Ahi/Ahimè is 'Ah', as the edition already renders it elsewhere; 'God,' is a modern casual oath.

old: God, how careful a man should be
new: Ah, how careful a man should be
why: Inf. XVI 118 'Ahi quanto cauti li uomini esser dienno'. Policy: Ahi = 'Ah'.

old: "lucky you, free to speak your mind.
new: "happy are you, to speak your mind so freely.
why: Inf. XVI 81 'felice te se sì parli a tua posta!' is a blessing (Longfellow: 'Happy art thou'); 'lucky you' is chatty and edges toward sarcasm.

old:
But his threat shamed me into courage,
the way a good master makes a servant brave.
new:
But shame made its threats to me,
as it makes a servant brave before a good master.
why: Inf. XVII 89-90 'ma vergogna mi fé le sue minacce, / che innanzi a buon segnor fa servo forte': shame threatens; Virgil made no threat.

old: "Damn it, you're dropping"
new: "Oh, you're coming down!"
why: Inf. XVII 129 'Omè, tu cali!' (Longfellow: 'Ah me, thou stoopest'); 'Damn it' is a modern oath, off register.

old: "Behold the beast
new: "Look at the beast
why: Inf. XVII 1 'Ecco la fiera'. Policy: leftover archaism; Ecco = 'Look'.

old: behold the one whose stench
new: look at the one whose stench
why: Inf. XVII 3 'ecco colei che tutto 'l mondo appuzza'. Policy: Ecco = 'look'.

old: God, how they made them lift their heels
new: Ah, how they made them lift their heels
why: Inf. XVIII 37 'Ahi come facean lor levar le berze'. Policy: Ahi = 'Ah'.

old: filthy, disheveled slut down there,
new: filthy, disheveled creature down there,
why: Inf. XVIII 130 'sozza e scapigliata fante': a low but not sexual word; Dante saves 'puttana' for the next tercet and 'slut' spends it early.

old: We had already climbed onto the next tomb,
new: We had already climbed, above the next ditch,
why: Inf. XIX 7 'a la seguente tomba' means the next bolgia; English 'tomb' sends the reader back to the heretics' sepulchres of IX-X.

old: Beneath my head are dragged the others down,
new: Beneath my head the others are dragged down,
why: Half-archaic inversion that trips aloud; Dante XIX 73 'Di sotto al capo mio son li altri tratti'.

old: "Whatever you want is good with me.
new: "Whatever pleases you pleases me.
why: Inf. XIX 37 'Tanto m'è bel, quanto a te piace' (Longfellow: 'What pleases thee, to me is pleasing'); 'is good with me' is current small talk.

old:
I do believe it pleased my guide:
he stood and listened the whole time
with such a satisfied look on his lips,
new:
I do believe it pleased my guide,
so satisfied was the look on his lips
the whole time he listened to the sound of those true words.
why: Realign on Dante's tercets: XIX 121-123 'I' credo ben ch'al mio duca piacesse, / con sì contenta labbia sempre attese / lo suon de le parole vere espresse.' Lectio spread 121-122 over three lines and pushed 123 into seg-0042.

old:
hearing the sound of those true words spoken.
So he took me up in both his arms,
and once he had me gathered to his chest,
new:
So he took me up in both his arms,
and once he had me gathered to his chest,
climbed back up the way he'd come down.
why: Realign: XIX 124-126 'Però con ambo le braccia mi prese; / e poi che tutto su mi s'ebbe al petto, / rimontò per la via onde discese.' Line moved up from seg-0043.

old:
climbed back up the way he'd come down.
He didn't tire of holding me clasped to him,
but carried me up to the crest of the arch
new:
He didn't tire of holding me clasped to him,
but carried me up to the crest of the arch
that crosses from the fourth bank to the fifth.
why: Realign: XIX 127-129 'Né si stancò … / sì men portò sovra 'l colmo de l'arco / che dal quarto al quinto argine è tragetto.' Line moved up from seg-0044.

old:
that crosses from the fourth bank to the fifth.
There he set his burden down with care,
with care, on the crag so steep and rough
new:
There he set his burden down with care,
with care, on the crag so steep and rough
it would have been hard going even for goats.
why: Realign: XIX 130-132 'Quivi soavemente spuose il carco, / soave per lo scoglio sconcio ed erto / che sarebbe a le capre duro varco.' Line moved up from seg-0045.

old:
it would have been hard going even for goats —
and from there another valley opened to me.
new: And from there another valley opened to me.
why: Realign: XIX 133 'Indi un altro vallon mi fu scoperto.' Policy: the canto's closing line stands alone in its own segment.

old: and we walked on the while.
new: and meanwhile we walked on.
why: Inf. XX 130 'e andavamo introcque'. Policy: leftover archaism ('the while').

old: twisted back toward the kidneys,
new: twisted round toward the small of the back,
why: Inf. XX 13 'da le reni era tornato 'l volto': reni is the loins, the lower back; 'kidneys' is anatomical and odd.

old: If I were a pane of leaded glass
new: If I were a mirror
why: Inf. XXIII 25 'S'i' fossi di piombato vetro': lead-backed glass, a mirror; a modern reader sees a stained-glass window and loses the reflection.

old: because of us — fooled, hurt, made fools of —
new: because of us, and hurt as well,
why: Inf. XXIII 14 'con danno e con beffa': injury and mockery; 'mocked' already stands in the line before, and 'fooled … made fools of' says it twice more.

old: more than a shift;
new: more than a nightgown;
why: Inf. XXIII 42 'una camiscia': she flees from bed; 'shift' is no longer common usage.

old: lying on down, or tucked under a quilt
new: sitting on feather cushions, or tucked under a quilt
why: Inf. XXIV 47 'seggendo in piuma' (Longfellow: 'sitting upon down'); aloud, 'lying on down' is heard as 'lying down'.

old: drew his back toward the temples,
new: drew his muzzle back toward the temples,
why: Inf. XXV 124 'Quel ch'era dritto, il trasse ver' le tempie': 'il' is the muzzle (muso, line 122); 'his back' reads as his spine.

old: to live like animals, dumb and grazing,
new: to live like beasts,
why: Inf. XXVI 119 'fatti non foste a viver come bruti': 'dumb and grazing' is added to one of the most quoted lines in the poem.

old: sought me out as the specialist
new: sought me out as his physician
why: Inf. XXVII 96 'così mi chiese questi per maestro / a guarir de la sua febbre superba': master in the sense of doctor; 'specialist' is modern clinical vocabulary.

old: that one going yonder dared
new: that one going off over there dared
why: Inf. XXX 43 'come l'altro che là sen va'. Policy: leftover archaism ('yonder').

old:
"so the other one
doesn't set its teeth in you — be so kind,
new:
"as you hope the other one
never sets its teeth in you, be so kind,
why: Inf. XXX 34-35 'se l'altro non ti ficchi / li denti a dosso' is an adjuration, 'so may the other not'; Lectio reads as a realization or purpose clause.

old: better for you if here you'd been sheep or goats.
new: better for you had you been sheep or goats on earth.
why: Inf. XXXII 15 'mei foste state qui pecore o zebe': 'qui' is here in the world where the poet writes; in this tercet 'here' reads as here in Hell.

old:
out of the water — back when
the peasant girl is dreaming of her gleaning
new:
out of the water, in the season
when the peasant girl dreams of her gleaning
why: Inf. XXXII 31-33 'quando sogna di spigolar sovente la villana': a season (early summer), not a past moment as 'back when' suggests.

old:
"Vexilla regis prodeunt inferni —
the banners of the king of Hell advance
toward us.
new:
"Vexilla regis prodeunt inferni
toward us.
why: Inf. XXXIV 1-2 'Vexilla regis prodeunt inferni / verso di noi' (Longfellow: 'Vexilla Regis prodeunt Inferni / Towards us'). Policy: Latin stays Latin with no in-line gloss; the added English line made the tercet four lines.

old: out of terror of him, drew the sea across itself
new: out of terror of him, made the sea its veil
why: Realign on Dante's tercets: XXXIV 121-123 end 'per paura di lui fé del mar velo'; 'for a veil' had spilled into seg-0042.

new:
and fled to our hemisphere; and maybe it was
to escape from him that what shows on this side
left its place here empty, and rushed back up."
why: Realign: XXXIV 124-126 'e venne a l'emisperio nostro; e forse / per fuggir lui lasciò qui loco vòto / quella ch'appar di qua, e sù ricorse.' Virgil's speech now closes with the tercet; 'rushed back' moved up from seg-0043.

old:
and rushed back, leaving the hollow behind it."
There is a place down there, as far from Beelzebub
as the limit of his tomb, made known to no one
new:
There is a place down there, as far from Beelzebub
as the limit of his tomb, made known to no one
by sight, but only by the sound
why: Realign: XXXIV 127-129 'Luogo è là giù da Belzebù remoto / tanto quanto la tomba si distende, / che non per vista, ma per suono è noto'. Narration now begins its own segment.

new:
of a little stream that trickles down there
through a hollow in the rock it has worn away
in its winding course, and it falls gently.
why: Realign: XXXIV 130-132 'd'un ruscelletto che quivi discende / per la buca d'un sasso, ch'elli ha roso, / col corso ch'elli avvolge, e poco pende.' Also breaks up the nineteen-syllable last line the report flagged.
